games.title: Hookworms (Ancylostoma duodenale & Necator americanus): quick quiz
games.blurb: Quiz for Year 2 and above, written fresh today.

questions.q: Which developmental stage of the hookworm is directly responsible for penetrating intact human skin to initiate infection?
questions.explanation: The third-stage (L3) filariform larva is the infective stage capable of actively penetrating human skin.

questions.q: A microscopic examination of an adult hookworm reveals two pairs of ventral teeth in its buccal capsule. Which organism is most likely present?
questions.explanation: Ancylostoma duodenale possesses ventral teeth in its buccal capsule, whereas Necator americanus features ventral cutting plates.

questions.q: A 30-year-old agricultural worker presents with severe fatigue, pallor, and pica. Laboratory tests reveal microcytic hypochromic anemia and eosinophilia. What is the primary pathophysiological mechanism causing anemia in this patient?
options: Intravascular hemolysis caused by parasite toxins
Chronic intestinal blood loss from mucosal attachment
Vitamin B12 malabsorption due to terminal ileum colonization
Bone marrow suppression secondary to larval migration
questions.explanation: Adult hookworms attach to the intestinal mucosa and feed on blood, causing chronic gastrointestinal blood loss and microcytic iron-deficiency anemia.

questions.q: What is the standard diagnostic method for confirming a hookworm infection in a clinical laboratory?
options: Microscopic identification of thin-shelled eggs in stool
Serological detection of specific IgE antibodies
Identification of filariform larvae in sputum samples
questions.explanation: Microscopic identification of characteristic thin-shelled, segmented eggs in stool is the primary diagnostic method for hookworm infection.

questions.q: Unlike Necator americanus, Ancylostoma duodenale can additionally be transmitted to humans through which of the following routes?
options: Oral ingestion of infective larvae and transmammary transmission
questions.explanation: Ancylostoma duodenale can be transmitted orally via contaminated food or water and transmammarily, unlike Necator americanus which relies almost exclusively on percutaneous penetration.

questions.q: Shortly after walking barefoot on damp soil, a patient develops an intense pruritic maculopapular eruption at the entry site, commonly termed 'ground itch'. What causes this manifestation?
options: Percutaneous penetration of L3 filariform larvae
Migration of adult worms into dermal capillaries
Egg deposition by adult females in subcutaneous tissue
Encystment of rhabditiform larvae in the epidermis
questions.explanation: Ground itch is a localized allergic skin reaction caused by percutaneous penetration of L3 filariform larvae.

questions.q: During the pulmonary migration phase of hookworm larvae, patients may present with transient dry cough, wheezing, and peripheral blood eosinophilia. What is this clinical condition called?
questions.explanation: Löffler syndrome describes transient respiratory symptoms and pulmonary infiltrates accompanied by peripheral eosinophilia caused by larval lung migration.

questions.q: Which of the following is the first-line anthelmintic pharmacological treatment for a confirmed hookworm infection?
questions.explanation: Benzimidazoles, such as albendazole or mebendazole, are the primary pharmacological agents used to clear hookworm infections.

questions.q: In stool samples left at room temperature, hookworm eggs may hatch into rhabditiform larvae. How are hookworm rhabditiform larvae morphologically distinguished from Strongyloides stercoralis rhabditiform larvae?
options: Hookworm larvae have a long buccal cavity and an inconspicuous genital primordium
Hookworm larvae have a short buccal cavity and a prominent genital primordium
Hookworm larvae possess a notched tail tip
questions.explanation: Hookworm rhabditiform larvae feature a long buccal cavity and small genital primordium, distinguishing them from Strongyloides larvae.

questions.q: Chronic, high-intensity hookworm infection in young children can lead to protein-losing enteropathy. Which laboratory abnormality is most characteristically associated with this severe complication?
questions.explanation: Severe chronic hookworm infection causes intestinal protein loss and blood depletion leading to hypoalbuminemia and peripheral edema.

games.title: Infantile Hypertrophic Pyloric Stenosis (IHPS): quick quiz
games.blurb: Quiz for Year 4 and above, written fresh today.

questions.q: What is the typical age of onset for symptoms in infants with hypertrophic pyloric stenosis?
questions.explanation: IHPS typically presents between 2 and 6 weeks of age with progressive non-bilious projectile vomiting.

questions.q: Which acid-base disturbance is classically associated with severe infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis?
questions.explanation: Persistent vomiting of gastric contents rich in hydrochloric acid leads to a hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis.

questions.q: What is the most appropriate initial imaging modality for diagnosing infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis?
questions.explanation: Abdominal ultrasound is the gold standard initial imaging modality as it avoids ionizing radiation and clearly visualizes the pyloric muscle dimensions.

questions.q: What ultrasound measurement of the pylorus is diagnostic for hypertrophic pyloric stenosis?
options: Pyloric muscle thickness > 3 mm and channel length > 14 mm
Pyloric muscle thickness < 1 mm and channel length < 5 mm
questions.explanation: Diagnostic criteria on ultrasound typically include a pyloric muscle thickness greater than 3 mm and a canal length greater than 14 mm.

questions.q: What is the definitive surgical treatment for infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis?
questions.explanation: Ramstedt pyloromyotomy involves splitting the hypertrophied pyloric muscle down to the submucosa without entering the lumen.

questions.q: What is the characteristic physical examination finding in an infant with hypertrophic pyloric stenosis?
options: A palpable, mobile, olive-shaped mass in the right upper quadrant
questions.explanation: The pathognomonic physical sign is the 'olive' mass, felt in the epigastrium or right upper quadrant, representing the hypertrophied pylorus.

questions.q: What type of vomiting is classically described in infants with pyloric stenosis?
questions.explanation: Obstruction occurs proximal to the ampulla of Vater, resulting in non-bilious, forceful projectile vomiting.

questions.q: Before proceeding to surgical correction of IHPS, what is the most critical management priority?
options: Immediate administration of broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics
Correction of fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base abnormalities
Insertion of a central venous catheter
questions.explanation: Resuscitation and correction of dehydration and electrolyte imbalances (especially hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis) are mandatory before anesthesia to prevent post-operative apnea.

questions.q: Which factor is considered an established risk factor for the development of infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis?
options: Exclusive breastfeeding for over one year
questions.explanation: IHPS is significantly more common in first-born male infants, with a male-to-female ratio of approximately 4:1.

questions.q: What is a common potential complication following a Ramstedt pyloromyotomy?
options: Incomplete pyloromyotomy resulting in persistent vomiting
Chronic malabsorption due to pancreatic insufficiency
questions.explanation: Incomplete division of the hypertrophied muscle fibers can lead to persistent postoperative vomiting, requiring repeat intervention.

games.title: Systemic sclerosis (2): case showdown
games.blurb: Case Showdown for Year 4 and above, written fresh today.

questions.q: A 48-year-old woman with diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis presents with severe headache, vision changes, and a blood pressure of 195/115 mmHg. Laboratory results show an elevated serum creatinine and microangiopathic hemolytic anemia. What is the most appropriate initial management step?
questions.explanation: Angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors such as captopril are the first-line treatment for scleroderma renal crisis and dramatically improve outcomes.

questions.q: A 42-year-old woman presents with skin tightening over her fingers, forearms, and face, along with Raynaud phenomenon and exertional dyspnea. Serological testing is positive for anti-topoisomerase I (anti-Scl-70) antibodies. Which complication is this patient at highest risk of developing?
questions.explanation: Anti-Scl-70 antibodies are characteristic of diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis and carry a high risk of pulmonary fibrosis/interstitial lung disease.

questions.q: A 55-year-old woman presents with long-standing Raynaud phenomenon, facial telangiectasias, esophageal dysphagia, and skin thickening restricted to her fingers and face. Serological evaluation is performed. Which autoantibody is most characteristically associated with this clinical presentation?
questions.explanation: Anti-centromere antibodies are strongly associated with limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis (CREST syndrome).

questions.q: A 60-year-old woman with systemic sclerosis presents with progressive fatigue and pale conjunctivae. Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy reveals longitudinal stripes of red, ectatic blood vessels radiating from the pylorus in the gastric antrum. What is the most likely diagnosis for this finding?
questions.explanation: Gastric antral vascular ectasia (GAVE, or 'watermelon stomach') is a recognized gastrointestinal complication of systemic sclerosis that presents with chronic occult blood loss and anemia.

questions.q: A 62-year-old woman with limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis presents with worsening exertional dyspnea and fatigue. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrates an estimated pulmonary artery systolic pressure of 58 mmHg with normal left ventricular ejection fraction and no significant left-sided heart disease. What is the most definitive diagnostic test to confirm the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Right heart catheterization is the gold standard required to definitively confirm the diagnosis of pulmonary arterial hypertension.

questions.q: A 50-year-old woman presents with rapidly progressive skin thickening over her trunk and proximal extremities over the past 3 months. Serological testing is positive for anti-RNA polymerase III antibodies. This antibody profile places her at the highest risk for which life-threatening complication?
questions.explanation: Anti-RNA polymerase III antibodies are strongly associated with diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis and carry a significantly increased risk of scleroderma renal crisis.

questions.q: A 38-year-old woman with systemic sclerosis presents with painful ischemic episodes in her fingers triggered by cold exposure, demonstrating sequential pallor, cyanosis, and erythema. Lifestyle measures including cold avoidance have failed to adequately control her symptoms. What is the first-line pharmacological treatment?
questions.explanation: Dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers, such as oral nifedipine, are the first-line pharmacological agent for Raynaud phenomenon.

questions.q: A 53-year-old man with recently diagnosed diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis presents with diffuse joint pain and severe hand swelling. The attending physician plans to initiate therapy for his musculoskeletal symptoms. High-dose systemic corticosteroid therapy should be avoided due to the risk of precipitating which acute condition?
questions.explanation: Moderate-to-high doses of systemic corticosteroids (>15 mg/day of prednisone equivalent) are a well-known risk factor for precipitating scleroderma renal crisis.

games.title: Viral haemorrhagic fevers: case showdown
games.blurb: Case Showdown for Year 4 and above, written fresh today.

questions.q: A 34-year-old male healthcare worker recently returned from the Democratic Republic of Congo presents with high fever, severe headache, myalgias, and subsequent watery diarrhea. Physical examination shows a maculopapular rash, conjunctival injection, and spontaneous bleeding from mucosal sites. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Recent travel to Central or West Africa with severe gastrointestinal distress, fluid loss, and hemorrhage in a healthcare worker is classic for Ebola virus disease.

questions.q: A 28-year-old female living in rural Nigeria presents with a 5-day history of fever, sore throat, severe retrosternal chest pain, and facial edema. Examination reveals pharyngeal exudates, subconjunctival hemorrhages, and significant proteinuria on urinalysis. What is the most likely underlying etiology?
questions.explanation: Lassa fever is an endemic West African arena-virus infection classically presenting with fever, exudative pharyngitis, retrosternal chest pain, facial swelling, and proteinuria.

questions.q: A 45-year-old male livestock farmer from Turkey presents with sudden-onset high fever, back pain, hepatomegaly, and extensive ecchymoses 4 days after removing a tick from his arm. Laboratory investigations demonstrate profound thrombocytopenia and elevated serum transaminases. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Tick exposure in Southern Europe, the Middle East, or Central Asia followed by acute fever, severe muscle/back pain, ecchymoses, and thrombocytopenia is indicative of Crimean-Congo haemorrhagic fever.

questions.q: A 22-year-old female returning from Southeast Asia presents with high fever, retro-orbital pain, and severe arthralgias. On day 5 of her illness, her fever subsides, but she develops severe abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, ascites, and a rapid increase in hematocrit alongside severe thrombocytopenia. What is the most critical next step in management?
options: Immediate intravenous fluid resuscitation with isotonic crystalloids
questions.explanation: The critical phase of severe dengue is characterized by systemic plasma leakage, making rapid, titrated intravenous fluid resuscitation with isotonic crystalloids the key life-saving intervention.

questions.q: A 31-year-old unvaccinated male traveler returns from the Amazon basin in Brazil with fever, chills, and myalgias that initially resolved, but he now presents with jaundice, hematemesis, oliguria, and relative bradycardia. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Yellow fever typically follows a biphasic course where initial symptoms resolve before severe hepatic damage (jaundice), renal failure, hematemesis, and Faget sign (pulse-temperature dissociation) develop.

questions.q: A 40-year-old male presents to an emergency department in the UK with high fever and melena 6 days after returning from an active viral hemorrhagic fever outbreak region in Africa. What is the immediate next best step in managing this patient?
options: Isolate patient in a single room with strict contact and droplet precautions
Administer empiric intravenous ribavirin before isolation
Order an urgent abdominal CT scan to evaluate melena
Discharge home with strict self-isolation instructions
questions.explanation: Immediate isolation in a single room with strict contact and droplet precautions using personal protective equipment is essential to prevent secondary transmission of suspected viral hemorrhagic fevers.

questions.q: A 38-year-old female tourist presents following a trip exploring bat-inhabited caves in Uganda with sudden high fever, severe headache, severe watery diarrhea, and a non-pruritic maculopapular rash on her trunk. On day 6 of illness, she develops bleeding from venipuncture sites and spontaneous ecchymoses. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Marburg virus disease is a filovirus infection associated with exposure to Egyptian fruit bat caves in Africa, presenting with rapid-onset fever, gastrointestinal distress, rash, and severe bleeding manifestations.

questions.q: A 50-year-old livestock worker in Kenya presents with acute fever, back pain, and confusion, followed by rapid vision loss in his left eye. Ophthalmoscopic examination reveals retinal hemorrhages and exudates. What is the most likely etiology?
questions.explanation: Rift Valley fever is transmitted from infected livestock and can present with acute hemorrhagic fever, encephalitis, and characteristic ocular complications such as retinitis and permanent visual loss.

games.title: Parasitology, Entomology and Bacteriology: drug duel
games.blurb: Drug Duel for Year 2 and above, written fresh today.

questions.q: A 32-year-old female is prescribed metronidazole for bacterial vaginosis. What is the primary mechanism of action of this drug?
options: Inhibition of bacterial cell wall peptidoglycan synthesis
Reduction to reactive intermediates that cause double-stranded DNA breakage in anaerobes
Binding to the 50S ribosomal subunit to block peptide bond formation
Inhibition of bacterial DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV
questions.explanation: Metronidazole is activated by anaerobic organisms to form nitro radical intermediates that damage bacterial DNA and cause cell death.

questions.q: Artemether is commonly used in combination therapy for uncomplicated Plasmodium falciparum malaria. Which of the following best describes its mechanism of action?
options: Generation of toxic endoperoxide free radicals that damage parasite organelles
Blockade of neuromuscular transmission by activating GABA receptors
Inhibition of protein synthesis by binding to the 30S ribosomal subunit
questions.explanation: Artemisinin derivatives contain an endoperoxide bridge that reacts with heme to generate reactive toxic free radicals inside the malaria parasite.

questions.q: A 7-year-old boy presents with intense nocturnal pruritus and interdigital web space burrows, diagnosed as scabies (Sarcoptes scabiei). Which drug is first-line topical treatment, and what is its mechanism of action?
options: Permethrin; voltage-gated sodium channel activation causing prolonged depolarization and parasite paralysis
Ivermectin; inhibition of bacterial cell wall synthesis
questions.explanation: Permethrin acts as a neurotoxin by delaying repolarization of neuronal sodium channels in ectoparasites like Sarcoptes scabiei, leading to paralysis.

questions.q: A patient returning from sub-Saharan Africa is diagnosed with Schistosoma haematobium infection. What is the mechanism of action of the drug of choice, praziquantel?
options: Increases parasite cell membrane permeability to calcium, causing muscular paralysis and tegumental disruption
Inhibits helminthic microtubule assembly by binding to beta-tubulin
Stimulates GABA-gated chloride channels in peripheral nerves
questions.explanation: Praziquantel induces rapid calcium influx across the trematode tegument, resulting in severe muscular contraction, paralysis, and parasite detachment.

questions.q: Which mechanism of action is responsible for the anti-helminthic activity of albendazole in treating Ascaris lumbricoides infections?
options: Inhibition of acetylcholinesterase at the neuromuscular junction
Selective inhibition of parasite beta-tubulin polymerization, preventing microtubule assembly
Activation of nicotinic acetylcholine receptors leading to spastic paralysis
questions.explanation: Albendazole binds selectively to helminthic beta-tubulin, blocking microtubule polymerization and disrupting glucose uptake and energy production.

questions.q: A patient receiving intravenous gentamicin for severe Gram-negative bacteremia must be monitored primarily for which pair of characteristic dose-dependent adverse effects?
questions.explanation: Aminoglycosides like gentamicin selectively accumulate in the renal cortex and inner ear fluid, causing potential nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity.

questions.q: Prior to prescribing primaquine for radical cure of dormant liver hypnozoites in Plasmodium vivax malaria, testing for which genetic condition is essential?
questions.explanation: Primaquine causes oxidative stress that can trigger severe hemolytic anemia in individuals with glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency.

questions.q: Oral vancomycin is indicated for the treatment of severe Clostridioides difficile colitis. What is its mechanism of action?
options: Binding to the D-alanyl-D-alanine terminus of cell wall peptidoglycan precursors to inhibit cell wall cross-linking
Inhibition of bacterial DNA-dependent RNA polymerase
Binding to the 50S ribosomal subunit to inhibit translocation
Competitive inhibition of bacterial dihydropteroate synthase
questions.explanation: Vancomycin is a glycopeptide antibiotic that binds D-ala-D-ala sequences in peptidoglycan monomers, preventing bacterial cell wall synthesis.

games.title: Respiratory Pathology: drug duel
games.blurb: Drug Duel for Year 3 and above, written fresh today.

questions.q: What is the primary mechanism of action of omalizumab, used in the management of severe persistent allergic asthma?
options: Monoclonal antibody that selectively binds to human immunoglobulin E (IgE)
questions.explanation: Omalizumab is a recombinant humanized monoclonal antibody that selectively binds to circulating IgE, preventing its interaction with high-affinity IgE receptors on mast cells and basophils.

questions.q: Which medication used to slow lung function decline in idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) acts as a intracellular receptor tyrosine kinase inhibitor?
questions.explanation: Nintedanib is a small-molecule tyrosine kinase inhibitor targeting platelet-derived growth factor receptors (PDGFR), fibroblast growth factor receptors (FGFR), and vascular endothelial growth factor receptors (VEGFR).

questions.q: A 42-year-old woman with pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) is started on bosentan. Which adverse effect requires regular monthly monitoring of routine laboratory parameters?
questions.explanation: Bosentan is a dual endothelin-receptor antagonist associated with dose-dependent hepatotoxicity, necessitating monthly baseline and maintenance serum transaminase monitoring.

questions.q: Which mechanism of action correctly describes roflumilast, an oral drug used as maintenance therapy for severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) with chronic bronchitis?
options: Long-acting antagonism of muscarinic M3 receptors
Up-regulation of beta-2 adrenergic receptor expression
questions.explanation: Roflumilast selectively inhibits PDE-4, increasing intracellular cAMP levels and suppressing inflammatory cell activity in patients with severe COPD.

questions.q: A patient receiving standard four-drug therapy for active pulmonary tuberculosis presents with decreased visual acuity and impaired red-green color discrimination. Which drug is responsible for this toxicity?
questions.explanation: Ethambutol causes optic neuritis, which characteristically presents as reduced visual acuity and retrobulbar neuritis affecting red-green color perception.

questions.q: What is the specific mechanism of action of ivacaftor in the treatment of cystic fibrosis in patients harboring the G551D mutation?
options: CFTR potentiator that increases the open-channel probability of surface CFTR proteins
CFTR corrector that promotes folding and cell membrane trafficking of F508del CFTR
Epithelial sodium channel (ENaC) inhibitor that enhances airway hydration
Recombinant human deoxyribonuclease that cleaves extracellular DNA in purulent sputum
questions.explanation: Ivacaftor is a CFTR potentiator that directly binds to surface CFTR channels with gating mutations (such as G551D) to increase channel open probability and chloride transport.

questions.q: What is the primary mechanism of action of montelukast in the management of asthma?
options: Competitive antagonism of cysteinyl leukotriene type 1 (CysLT1) receptors
questions.explanation: Montelukast selectively blocks the CysLT1 receptor, preventing leukotriene D4-mediated bronchoconstriction, airway edema, and inflammatory cell recruitment.

questions.q: Which anti-tuberculosis drug acts primarily by inhibiting bacterial DNA-dependent RNA polymerase?
questions.explanation: Rifampicin binds to the beta subunit of bacterial DNA-dependent RNA polymerase, thereby suppressing RNA synthesis in Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
